fields.why: If one actor writes the test, writes the code, runs it and reports the result, the last step is a claim, and nothing has been established. The false greens that actually happen are not forged: they are an agent that honestly believes it succeeded, and a check that exits 0 having asserted nothing (a success flag, a help-text match, a mocked dependency). Both look identical to a real green afterwards. 0.2 rebuilt the author/observer separation as a spine after collapsing to one agent loop removed it; 0.3 keeps the lesson, not the spine.
fields.title: The author of the work is not its only witness
fields.statement: A green is credible only when the party that produced the work is not the only party that observed the result. The author's own report that it passed is an opinion; the proof is a run someone else can repeat and see fail and pass — a test watched going red then green, and CI verifying the merge with main.
fields.howToApply: Ask who ESTABLISHED the fact, not whether it is asserted. Before trusting a new check, ask what input would make it red, produce that input, and watch it fail. Never report 'tests pass' from memory or from a summary — cite the run. Treat CI on the merge with main as the verdict, not your local run. Pin the observable outcome, never a flag or exit code standing in for it.
fields.description: Whoever authored the work does not get to be the only witness that it worked.

fields.title: Pull-based context architecture
fields.problem: Pre-loading a big static brief pays three costs every turn: a context tax (most of it is irrelevant to the step), staleness (a snapshot taken at session start does not reflect later edits), and one-size-fits-all (no step gets context tailored to it). Static instruction is also followed less reliably than context pulled at the step that needs it.
fields.approach: Thin bootstrap: generated guidance (CLAUDE.md, role files) names surfaces and how to reach them, not their contents. Pull on demand: `storytree library search|read|links`, or the agent link's search_notes and record reads, always reading current state. Progressive disclosure: each read points at the next thing worth fetching. Keep briefs to subagents lean: self-contained means complete pointers, not complete payloads. When one context to pull still exceeds the window, decompose instead of summarising lossily: hand a subagent the query, let it filter to the relevant slice in its own window, and take back a cited digest.
fields.statement: Give an agent a thin bootstrap — its role, current objective, and how to fetch more — and let it pull exactly the context its current step needs, from the live source, on demand. Pointers, not payloads.
fields.tradeoffs: A guaranteed-complete upfront snapshot, traded for freshness and a small initial load; the agent makes extra fetches, each reading live state. The cost of the model: a session cannot pull an artifact to decide whether it needs it, so a few judgement calls (whether to fan out, whether to escalate) must live in the thin bootstrap itself.
fields.description: Brief an agent thinly and let it pull fresh context just-in-time, rather than pushing a fat static brief at session start.

fields.why: Escalating feels careful and costs the escalating session nothing; the whole cost lands on the owner's turns, the one resource that does not scale. The owner objected four times in 0.2 ('this feels like you're asking me to stamp something I asked to be done'); in one walkthrough three of seven questions got answers wider than asked. The failing sessions read the clauses accurately — the missing step was asking why the clause existed. Decisions are a record of reasoning, not constitutional law.
fields.title: Read the force a decision answered, not the clause it left behind
fields.statement: When a clause in an accepted decision seems to refuse the work in front of you, its authority is the FORCE it answered — what would go wrong if it were ignored — not the sentence. Name that force and take one of three exits: (A) it still holds here → comply, and say which force; (B) it is dead → the clause is stale prose, and correcting the record is your move; (C) it holds but the clause is a deferral ('not decided here', 'a separate larger decision', 'pending') whose answer somebody can PRODUCE → do the work that answers it. Only a genuine owner call — taste, spend, an irreversible or outward-facing act — goes to the owner.
fields.howToApply: First check it is a CLAUSE, not a wall: a mechanism that refuses (CI, a claim refusal, a failing test) is not this rule's subject — comply. Only an accepted decision's prose is. Step 1: state the force in one sentence without reusing the clause's words; if you can only restate it, you have not found it — read further (Context/Consequences), do not proceed either way. Step 2: take exit A, B or C. For C, look for a precedent that already answered the same question for a neighbour. Test: would the owner answer 'I already told you to do that'? Then it was never his. Whatever exit you take, keep the reason in the record. No exit ever licenses skipping a test, CI or review — this rule can only remove an owner question, never a proof.
fields.description: A decision's clause binds only while the force it answered still holds — read the why before complying or escalating.

fields.why: A test that has never been seen to fail is not evidence — writing the implementation first invites tests shaped to pass vacuously. Watching it go red proves it actually exercises the behaviour.
fields.title: Red-green
fields.statement: A failing (red) test is written and seen to fail before the implementation that turns it green.
fields.howToApply: Write the test, run it and watch it fail for the reason you expect (not a syntax error or an unrelated break), then write the smallest implementation that turns it green. Under minimal viable TDD the test must protect a product behaviour; red-green is how you know it does.
fields.description: Author the failing test before the implementation that turns it green.

fields.why: Restated prose drifts: copy a rule into N bodies and one edit leaves N-1 stale copies, with no reader knowing which is canonical. 0.1 encoded this twice and 0.2 made the library the one copy; 0.3's library is the edit surface and files are generated from it, so a link costs nothing and buys one-edit propagation.
fields.title: Reference, don't restate
fields.statement: A durable rule lives ONCE, as a library note; every consumer — a role, a story, a report, generated guidance — links to it instead of restating it in its own prose.
fields.howToApply: Before writing rule prose into any body, search the library (`storytree library search`). If a note covers it, link it with at most a one-line gloss of why it binds here — and open the note before writing the gloss, because a link riding beside a claim makes the claim look checked. If none does, write the note and link it. A consumer keeps only what is its own: role, boundaries, workflow shape, links. Smell test: if two bodies could share a paragraph, that paragraph is a note.
fields.description: Durable discipline lives once in the library; every other surface links to it rather than copying it.

fields.why: In 0.2 the owner asked what was left on an arc, got an accurate answer, and replied 'can you rephrase with less jargon'; the same facts rephrased got 'this is much easier to read'. Register was the only variable. The owner is not a newcomer — he holds the intent and history better than any session; what he lacks is the machine vocabulary. 'Explain it to a newcomer' produces padding, the worse failure. And ids are how sessions hand off precisely, so this licenses no vagueness in notes.
fields.title: Register follows audience
fields.statement: Choose register by AUDIENCE: compressed and identifier-dense for notes and agent-to-agent handoff; for the OWNER, translate the machine vocabulary — ids, lifecycle terms, decision numbers, internal names — naming each thing by what it DOES, leading with the answer or the ask, and never re-explaining the project he set.
fields.howToApply: A DECISION for the owner: stakes first, every term glossed, options with both sides of each trade-off, a non-binding recommendation, an analogy that says where it breaks, a diagram when the subject is a structure or flow, at most one question — and put it on an open question raised on the arc, not only in chat. A MID-SESSION UPDATE: the answer or ask in sentence one; items named by what they do, id in parentheses at most; decided work split from work needing his call. The LANDING DEBRIEF: what landed (PR numbers + a plain outcome paragraph) and whether the session is safe to close, yes or no. RE-ONBOARDING a cold owner: where things stand, what he needs to know, what you make of it, what you want from him. Offer the analogy or diagram unasked — being asked for one is the failure signal.
fields.description: Translate machine vocabulary for the owner; keep it compressed and precise between agents.

fields.title: Render and witness a flag-guarded surface
fields.problem: Two failure modes. (1) Reaching for a screenshot where an assertion would do — 'the path starts at the dock and never self-intersects' is a geometry assertion; 'the panel shows X given these props' is a component test. (2) For the part that needs an eye, hand-writing a throwaway capture script each run, re-hitting the same traps (a hidden browser tab suspends rendering and hangs the screenshot) and producing evidence no two runs agree on.
fields.approach: 1. Push machine facts down: geometry invariants and render/behaviour facts become tests; use DOM/computed-style inspection to turn an eyeballed fact into an assertion. What remains is the look. 2. Witness with a committed capability: the repo's Playwright/e2e harness for the desktop app, with deterministic settling (wait for app-reported settled state, never sleep), a visible or headless page, and deterministic rendering so the witness is repeatable. If no harness covers the surface, build one once rather than a per-run script. 3. Keep it feedback: build the look behind a flag, capture it, stand the experience up for the owner, and stop. Only the owner's attestation moves the look to done; the builder never self-signs it.
fields.statement: A visual builder checks its work by witnessing a flag-guarded surface, but the witness is FEEDBACK, never the proof: first turn every machine-checkable visual fact into a test, then witness only the irreducible look with the repo's committed capture harness, and stop for the owner's look verdict.
fields.tradeoffs: A committed harness is less nimble than a bespoke one-off script, but pays for itself by the second use. The sharper risk is the inverse over-reach: treating a green self-captured screenshot as if it proved the look.
fields.description: A visual builder's own screenshots are feedback, never a verdict: push machine-checkable visual facts into tests, witness the rest with a committed harness, and hand the owner a working surface to attest.

fields.why: Story-author owns WHAT, so a structural fork already has an owner who is not the human. In 0.2 a package-layout fork was put to the owner, who corrected: 'the answer to these questions should belong to story writer not to me'; routed to story-author it was decided cleanly and landed green. Escalating it spends the owner's scarcest channel on a question the corpus already routes elsewhere and stalls the work.
fields.title: Route structural forks to story-author, not the owner
fields.statement: A fork whose subject is the WORK HIERARCHY — which package owns what, dependency edges, where a module lives, story/capability boundaries, whether a new story is needed — is decided by the story-author role, not escalated to the owner. Raise it to the owner only if the structural call is genuinely irreversible, outward-facing, or unsettleable from the decision log.
fields.howToApply: When a unit hinges on a structural, package, dependency or boundary call, spawn story-author to decide and author it (plan_story / plan_capability), then record the decision (accepted when the owner directed it in the conversation). The discriminator is the SUBJECT of the fork, not your confidence: 'I'm unsure which package owns this' is still story-author's call.
fields.description: Package layout, dependency edges and story boundaries are the story-author's call, not the owner's.

fields.steps:
1. Ask what MAIN's code infers, not what your branch needs: find every query on main that names or infers the thing you would drop (an ON CONFLICT target errors the moment its index is gone).
2. Never swap in one edit: a drop+add in one landing has no safe moment - applied early it breaks every older writer, withheld it leaves your branch red.
3. EXPAND in its own PR: additive schema only, the old shape still standing, AND every writer moved to the new target.
4. MIGRATE in that same PR: backfill with values correct for existing rows; every statement a no-op on re-run, and the fresh-install path and the upgrade path must produce the identical shape.
5. CONTRACT in a later PR, once no running code still infers the old shape (installed apps included). When you cannot establish that, leave the overlap - a redundant index is cheap.
6. If no compatible overlap exists, name the break window (who breaks, for how long) and escalate; never take a silent one.
fields.title: Migrate a library schema: expand, migrate, contract
fields.trigger: You are about to change the project schema in a way that drops or narrows something: a primary key, a unique constraint or index an ON CONFLICT infers, a foreign-key target, a column, a NOT NULL. Purely additive changes (new table, new column with a default) do not arm it.
fields.surfaces: The library package's project schema and its apply-on-open; every writer whose SQL names a constraint; separate PRs through the merge ceremony.
fields.statement: The project schema is applied on every open of a project library, and more than one version of the code opens the same library: the app that follows merged main, your branch's tests and tools, a sibling session's branch, and a user's older installed app. So a change that drops or narrows something running code relies on lands in steps: EXPAND (add the new shape beside the old and move every writer onto it), MIGRATE (backfill, guarded, re-runnable), then CONTRACT (drop the old shape) in a later PR.
fields.description: A schema change that drops or narrows something lands as expand, then migrate, then contract, in separate PRs - never a one-shot swap.
fields.failureModes:
- A constraint swap treated as one atomic edit: in 0.2 a primary-key swap left the branch red against the shared store while applying it would have broken main's claim writes for every other session.
- Reading "idempotent" as "safe": a guarded, re-runnable swap is still incompatible with the code already running.
- Contracting in the same PR that expanded.
- Fresh-install and upgrade paths that diverge, so two openers disagree about what the table is.

fields.why: This is the problem storytree exists for. An operator running several agent sessions is flooded, not starved; the only options were 'read everything' (the operator is the bottleneck again) or 'trust it' (discovery deferred to runtime). A middle exists only if something takes a position on what deserves attention now. A position is a claim that can be examined and overruled, unlike a summary whose omissions look like absences. The owner's correction: storytree IS opinionated and MAY hide paths, but rarely — 99% of the time there is a visible way.
fields.title: Show what matters at the stage they are at
fields.statement: A surface shows the operator what matters AT THE STAGE THEY ARE ACTUALLY AT — the system holds an opinion about that and acts on it, including by hiding what this stage does not need — and because that opinion can be wrong, there is always one consistent way to overrule it.
fields.howToApply: Ask what stage the reader is at before asking what to show: at THIS stage, does this change what the operator does next? Rank before you hide; hiding is the expensive, declared exception with a stated reason. Never hide that you hid — the fact of an opinion stays visible, with an always-present escape hatch reachable from where the operator hit the wall, not buried in settings.
fields.description: A surface takes a position on what deserves the operator's attention now — and always leaves one way to overrule it.

fields.why: An agent works in a finite attention window. Every sentence that does not help it choose the next move competes with the sentences that do; low-signal guidance does not merely fail to help, it crowds out what would.
fields.title: Signal and noise
fields.statement: Judge any guidance an agent reads by its discriminatory power — signal lets the agent tell the correct action from the alternatives; noise consumes attention without adding that power — and author for high signal.
fields.howToApply: High signal is actionable, specific (concrete files, commands, decisions), verifiable, and grounded in the code as it is. Noise is meta-talk, stale context, generic philosophy and restatement. Per sentence ask: can I remove it without lowering the chance the task completes? Does it point to a specific action or criterion? Is it said elsewhere (link the one source)? Will it still be true later?
fields.description: Judge guidance by discriminatory power: keep what helps an agent choose the right move, cut the rest.

fields.why: The black-box complaint was never that tools show too little; it is that what they show is generated rather than measured — a narration by the same thing doing the work, structurally unable to contradict it, and most confident exactly where it is least informed. It is also what makes the surface's opinionatedness affordable: ranking measurements is triage; ranking guesses is a confident guess with fewer options.
fields.title: Signals must be real
fields.statement: Everything a surface shows is ANCHORED TO REAL CODE AND REAL TELEMETRY — a signal is a READING TAKEN FROM the system, never a DESCRIPTION OF the system produced alongside it.
fields.howToApply: For every element, name what it was read FROM — the file, the record, the event, the test run. If you cannot, it is decoration: remove it. Prefer an honest 'unknown' to a plausible placeholder. Beware a signal computed from its own subject: ask what state of the world would turn it red; if none, it measures nothing. Staleness is allowed; undisclosed staleness is not — a snapshot says when it was taken. Rollups of real readings are real; prose is fine unless it presents as a reading.
fields.description: Everything a surface shows is a reading taken from real code and telemetry, never a description generated alongside it.

fields.why: Source built ahead of a proving test is unproven surface: an interface with one implementation, a dependency no test demanded, a refactor smuggled into a fix all add behaviour no red test pinned, so the tests attest to less than what shipped.
fields.title: Slow growth: the minimum to green
fields.statement: Write the minimum source that turns the failing test (or the small cluster of tests you just wrote) green — no speculative abstraction, no speculative dependency, no wide refactor disguised as a fix.
fields.howToApply: Pick the red test(s); make the smallest change in the owning package that turns them green; iterate. Every test the source answers to exists before the source does. Smells: an interface with a single implementation, a package added without naming the test that demands it, a diff touching files no failing test reaches.
fields.description: Write the minimum source that turns the failing test green — no speculative abstraction, dependency or refactor.

fields.why: Premature splits fragment a journey and multiply seams; refusing to split leaves units whose outcome is a list and whose proof is two unrelated walkthroughs stapled together. Two falsifiable triggers make the call testable rather than aesthetic.
fields.title: The splitting rule
fields.statement: Split a story, capability or contract only when EITHER its outcome cannot be stated in one sentence without conjunctions, OR its proof does not share a common precondition and observable.
fields.howToApply: Tiebreakers — split if two or more hold: distinct REAL user populations (not role labels worn by the same person), two separate rebuild briefs, a spike mixed with delivery, an internal contradiction. Length is NEVER a splitting criterion. After deciding to split, re-check each side is still one coherent journey.
fields.description: Split a unit only when its outcome needs conjunctions or its proof shares no common precondition and observable; length never counts.

fields.steps:
1. Start it yourself from the right directory with the right runner (dev server, desktop app, built site). A bare shell line punted to the owner broke in his environment once (wrong cwd, a local dependency not on PATH) and he had to debug it before he could test; his direction was to have it up and running so he can simply test.
2. Probe, do not assume: an HTTP 2xx on the entry route, a rendered marker, or a screenshot of the actual surface. If it will not serve, that is yours to fix or escalate.
3. Hand over the confirmed link, the exact thing to open or try, and the specific question to rule on; the question itself goes on the arc as an open question.
4. Never record the owner's verdict yourself because you made it easy to give.
fields.title: Stage the owner's look
fields.trigger: A unit reaches a point only an owner look can settle (appearance, feel, a live check he must witness).
fields.surfaces: The session's own dev servers / app launch and the probe that confirms them; the handoff message; an open question on the arc.
fields.statement: When a unit needs the owner to look at, feel or try something running - a visual surface, an interaction, a desktop build - the session starts it, verifies it is genuinely serving, and hands the owner a confirmed-working URL or entry point plus a short "what to judge". A raw command is only a fallback. The owner still gives the verdict; you remove the friction, not the judgment.
fields.description: When the owner must see something running to judge it, start it yourself, prove it serves, and hand over a working link plus what to judge.
fields.failureModes:
- Handing over a command instead of a running experience.
- "I ran the start command so it is up" - the server never bound, the build 404s, or a hidden browser tab stalls.
- Signing the look-and-feel verdict yourself.
- Spinning up servers for every message: this is for the moment the owner must witness something.

fields.why: A stateful rule promoted to guidance misfires in every context lacking its hidden state, and guidance is read by every future session, so a wrong graduation spreads exactly as far as a right one. The asymmetry favours withholding: leaving a stateless item another round costs one round; graduating a stateful one costs every reader until someone notices.
fields.title: Stateless graduates, stateful stays
fields.statement: Only a STATELESS rule — one that applies the same way on every read, with no dependence on prior sessions, host paths or accumulated context — graduates into durable guidance; STATEFUL context stays where it is, and UNCERTAIN withholds.
fields.howToApply: When graduating memory into the library, classify each candidate: STATELESS → candidate; STATEFUL (a path, a date-bound state, a one-session recipe) → stays in memory; UNCERTAIN → withhold. State the classification in every proposal — it is the load-bearing logic, not a formality.
fields.description: Only stateless rules graduate from memory into library guidance; stateful context stays ephemeral, and uncertainty withholds.

fields.why: A test is only as good as the observable it pins. Checking that a file exists (not its contents), that a function was called (not what it produced), or that a flag is true (not the result it claims) gives a green with no proof behind it — and an agent rewarded for green will satisfy exactly that hollow signal. Fixtures fail the same way: a whole-module mock deletes the real library's runtime guards (0.2: 885/885 green while the real library threw), and hand-built small numbers cannot discriminate a rule that breaks at production scale.
fields.title: Test creation principles
fields.statement: A test must verify the actual outcome rather than a proxy for it — real content over existence, user-facing behaviour over implementation detail — and must genuinely fail if the behaviour it pins were removed.
fields.howToApply: The deletion check first: if the feature were removed, would this test fail? If not, it pins nothing. Assert produced content and behaviour, including the unhappy path; avoid permissive assertions (length > 0), success-flag-only checks, swallowed errors. Under minimal viable TDD a test earns its place by protecting a product behaviour — no tests of decision records, prose, retirements or repo structure. Prefer real collaborators (0.3's tests get a throwaway local Postgres); when you must mock, pin the options the real dependency requires and make fixture values span production magnitudes. Never assert a wall-clock duration — on a shared box it measures CPU starvation; use an injected clock. Make an environment-bound test's skip visible (a skip option, not an `if` around the declaration), so a test that did not run is never counted as proof.
fields.description: A test verifies the real outcome, not a proxy, and must fail if the behaviour it pins were removed.

fields.why: Two jobs get confused. Deciding whether something needs you is triage and is the system's job — making the operator click through a hierarchy to find out is 'review everything' with nicer graphics. Deciding how far to go is investigation and is the operator's — depth is only a cost when it is compulsory. The owner's words: 'you choose which rabbit hole to jump into and how far to go down.' A drill-down gives depth without selection; a search box gives selection without depth; neither is the in-between.
fields.title: The reader chooses the thread and the depth
fields.statement: TRIAGE IS PUSHED AND INVESTIGATION IS PULLED — the system decides WHAT NEEDS the operator's attention, and the operator decides WHICH thread to follow and HOW FAR DOWN it to go.
fields.howToApply: Separate the two jobs before designing either: triage arrives unbidden, investigation never does. Count clicks to a decision (target zero), not clicks to the bottom. Every level must answer something on its own — a level that exists only to be passed through is a toll. Offer more than one way in. Treat stopping as success. A suggestion of where to look next is fine; 'show more' of the same level is not another level.
fields.description: Triage is pushed and investigation is pulled: the system says what needs attention; the operator chooses which thread and how deep.

fields.why: When the resting view is derived from bounds, padding and a projection, there is always a true sentence available — this is what the function returns — which answers a question nobody asked. In 0.2 a projection change left half the modules on old assumptions and the map silently opened ~28x smaller; every piece was defensible, the composition nobody owned was not, and there was no stated framing for the new one to contradict. An undesigned view cannot be regressed.
fields.title: The resting view is designed, not fitted
fields.statement: The RESTING COMPOSITION of a visual surface — the camera, zoom and framing a reader arrives at — is a DESIGNED state someone chose and can defend. A camera or fit function that merely contains the content has computed a view, not designed one, and 'the fit computes it' never answers whether the view is right.
fields.howToApply: Ask who decided the framing, against what intent (how much of the whole is visible, what dominates, what the margins are for). Treat any change that moves the resting composition — projection maths, bounds, padding, camera elevation, a sizing constant — as a change to the composition, and give it the owner's look. When a view is derived, pin what it must satisfy: a stated share of the frame, a minimum on-screen size for the primary object, or a reference capture. Views the reader navigated to themselves are theirs, not the surface's.
fields.description: The composition a reader arrives at is a decision someone made; 'the fit function computes it' is not evidence it is right.

fields.why: The trees look like one repository and behave like several, and tools report success either way. In 0.2 a session wrote a whole increment (nine files) into the primary checkout while working in a worktree; its own `git status` was clean, so its honesty check passed while the edits landed on a divergent baseline. The read half is quieter: a session read a schema through the primary checkout's path and got a version two decisions old. Absolute paths copied from briefs and memory never look environment-specific, and subagents inherit the slip with the path.
fields.title: The same file in another tree is a different file
fields.statement: A repository checked out more than once — the primary checkout plus every worktree, and in 0.3's training-wheels period two repositories side by side — has one path per tree and different bytes behind each. Resolve every path against THIS session's own root, and never read another tree's content, clean status or green test as evidence about your branch.
fields.howToApply: Establish the root once from the session: `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` in your own directory. Treat any path from a brief, memory file or earlier session as a recollection. Worktrees live under the primary root, so 'starts with the primary path' proves nothing — the longest matching root wins. After a write, a clean status in your tree is not confirmation; check where it landed. Give every subagent your absolute root explicitly and check both trees when it returns. Before a read becomes a premise, know which commit that tree is on.
fields.description: In a worktree session, resolve every path against your own tree's root; another checkout's bytes and status are not evidence about your branch.

fields.why: A tightened validator can break fixtures or data anywhere that leaned on the old looser behaviour, and that surfaces at runtime, not at typecheck — so the change compiles, the owning package is green, and the break lands elsewhere. In 0.3 tests run only what a change can reach, so this is the case where you must widen the run deliberately. The sweep half: in 0.2 a migration searched for the tag `witness: human`, reported 'none remain', and missed five untagged items the parser defaulted to exactly that value — the blind spot pointed straight at the units the sweep existed for.
fields.title: Tightening a shared contract needs a full sweep
fields.statement: When a change makes a shared parser, schema or validator reject inputs it used to accept, run the tests of EVERY package that consumes it before landing — not just the owner's. And whenever a sweep will claim completeness, derive its scope by enumerating every unit and resolving each one's value through the real parser, never by searching for the marker.
fields.howToApply: Tightening (reject more)? Run `pnpm test` across all consumers of the contract, or the full suite; a red sibling blocks the landing. Loosening cannot break an existing fixture, so it does not trigger. For a sweep: enumerate the universe, parse each unit with the production parser, bucket by resolved value, and check the buckets sum to the total. Ask what an ABSENT value defaults to — if it defaults to the value you are sweeping for, a marker search misses every one.
fields.description: When a shared validator starts rejecting what it accepted, test every consumer; scope any completeness-claiming sweep by enumerating units, never by grepping a marker.

fields.why: A unit extracted for a single consumer is indirection with no reuse payoff: it adds a hop for every reader, splits authority between the unit and its lone consumer, and bets context budget on a future that may never come.
fields.title: Two-consumer extraction
fields.statement: Extract shared content into its own unit only when two or more CURRENT consumers share it — one consumer plus a hoped-for second is speculation, not extraction.
fields.howToApply: Count actual consumers before extracting and name them in the new note. Below two, leave the content where it lives. This is the complement of reference-dont-restate: that rule says link, don't copy, once a note exists; this one says when a note should exist at all.
fields.description: Extract shared content into its own note only when two or more current consumers share it.

fields.why: Chasing surface coverage authors unproven breadth — tests no red ever demanded — whereas a defect-driven list keeps every case earned by a real failure. This is the story-level form of minimal viable TDD, carried from 0.2's UAT practice (a CLI proven by running a few core commands, a store by a successful data pull).
fields.title: A story's proof proves the goal, not the surface
fields.statement: A story's end-to-end proof shows its OUTCOME — it does not cover the surface. Author the minimal case that proves the goal against real collaborators; the list grows only when a real defect earns a permanent regression case.
fields.howToApply: Ship one test that proves the story's goal end to end with real collaborators. Add a case only when a real defect surfaces, and keep it permanently. If a surface genuinely cannot be settled by code or a driver (a taste judgement), say so explicitly rather than skipping it silently — but an un-harnessed surface is a build task, not a reason to skip.
fields.description: Prove the story's outcome with the minimal end-to-end case; grow the list one case per real defect.
